Bruit
BROOT
noun
From the French bruit, a noise or report, from Old French bruire (to roar, to make a din); a bruit is a rumor, a report, the noised tidings of a thing.

Biblical Definition

A bruit is a report, a rumor, the noised tidings of some great and commonly dreadful thing. The word appears but twice in the KJV, and both times it carries the sound of coming judgment. Jeremiah cries, “Behold, the noise of the bruit is come, and a great commotion out of the north country, to make the cities of Judah desolate” (Jer 10:22) — the rumor of the invader running before his armies, the very report a terror. And Nahum, pronouncing Nineveh’s doom, says, “all that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee” (Nah 3:19) — the report of the tyrant’s fall greeted with applause by the nations he had ground down. So the bruit is tidings that travel ahead of a fate: in Judah, the dread of judgment approaching; in Nineveh, the joy of judgment fallen. Scripture treats such reports soberly. “Thou shalt not raise a false report” (Exo 23:1); and the righteous man “shall not be afraid of evil tidings: his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD” (Psa 112:7). Here is the believer’s stay against every fearful bruit: rumors of war and ruin may run, and the wicked have cause to dread the report of their end, but the man whose heart is fixed on God need not be moved by the loudest rumor. The bruit that terrifies the guilty cannot unsettle the trusting.

Webster 1828 Definition

Report; rumor; noised tidings, commonly of some fearful or notable event.

expand to see more

BRUIT, n. [French bruit, a noise.] Report; rumor; fame; the noised tidings of a thing.

The loud running of a report through a country, especially of war, disaster, or a great man’s fall.

BRUIT, v.t. To report; to noise abroad; to spread the rumor of.

Akin in sense to fame and rumor, but with the ring of a din or outcry in it.

In Scripture, twice used, and both of a dreadful report — Judah’s invader and Nineveh’s downfall.

Key Scripture

Jer 10:22 — "Behold, the noise of the bruit is come, and a great commotion out of the north country, to make the cities of Judah desolate, and a den of dragons."

Nah 3:19 — "There is no healing of thy bruise; thy wound is grievous: all that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?"

Exo 23:1 — "Thou shalt not raise a false report: put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness."

Psa 112:7 — "He shall not be afraid of evil tidings: his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Not a doctrine in dispute but a vanished word; ‘bruit’ recovers the fixed heart that fears no evil tidings because it trusts the LORD.

expand to see more

The word rebukes the fear that feeds on rumor. Our age is drowned in bruits — every hour a fresh report of alarm, and hearts made captive to tidings they cannot verify or govern. Scripture does not deny that dreadful reports come; Judah heard the bruit of the north and it was real. But it forbids the false report (Exo 23:1) and fortifies the believer against the true one: ‘his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD’ (Psa 112:7). The wicked have cause to dread the bruit of their end; the child of God, though he hear the loudest rumor, is not moved, for his life is hid in One the rumor cannot reach.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has simply fallen out of use, and with it a vivid name for the running of fearful report. Recover the principle beneath it: evil tidings will come, but a heart fixed on the LORD is not to be shaken by any bruit, and false reports are not to be raised or received.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A French word for noise and report, come whole into English and kept only in the KJV and the old speech.

expand to see more

bruire (Old French) — to roar, rustle, make a din; the sound behind the word.

bruit (French noun) — noise, and thence rumor or report; borrowed unchanged into English.

Kin in idea: rumor, fame, report, tidings — all of a thing spread by hearsay.

The Hebrew behind Jer 10:22 (shemuah) and Nah 3:19 (shema) means simply ‘a thing heard,’ a report.

Both biblical uses are of judgment — dreaded as it approaches, applauded when it falls on the tyrant.

Usage

"The bruit of the invader ran before his armies, and Judah trembled."

"All that heard the bruit of Nineveh’s fall clapped their hands."

"Let the bruits run: the heart fixed on the LORD is not afraid of evil tidings."
